questions.q: Identify the punctuation mark used repeatedly in the play to indicate pauses, hesitation, or trailing thoughts in Derry's speech, and give one example from the text.
questions.a: The ellipsis (…) is used repeatedly to show Derry's hesitation, emotional pauses, and incomplete thoughts. Example: "I....there....I thought this was an empty place." A wrong answer (e.g., "comma" or "dash") reveals the student hasn't noticed how punctuation maps onto psychological state — a critical skill for drama analysis in board exams.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how Mr Lamb's use of imperative sentences ("Mind the apples," "Look over there") differs in function from Derry's use of interrogatives ("What? Who's that?" "Why don't you ask me?").
questions.a: Mr Lamb's imperatives guide attention outward — to the garden, to observation, to action — reflecting his engagement with the world. Derry's interrogatives turn inward, demanding explanations, challenging perceptions, revealing defensiveness and a need to control the narrative. A wrong answer that only labels sentence types without linking to character psychology shows surface-level understanding.

questions.q: In the exchange where Derry says "People are afraid of me" and Mr Lamb replies "Why should that be?", rewrite Derry's next long speech as a single complex sentence using a subordinate clause, then explain what is lost in the transformation.
questions.a: Rewritten: "Because everyone thinks my face is the ugliest thing they ever saw and looks at me with pity that masks fear, I know people are afraid of me." Lost: the staccato rhythm ("You think.... 'Here's a boy.' You look at me...and then you see my face...") that mimics Derry's spiraling anxiety and the dramatic pauses that let the audience feel his pain. A student who only combines sentences grammatically misses the performative dimension of dramatic language.

questions.q: Compare the register (level of formality) in Mr Lamb's speech ("I should say....to look at it.... I should say, you got burned in a fire") with Derry's ("Not in a fire. I got acid all down that side of my face and it burned it all away"). What does this contrast reveal about their relationship to their own disabilities?
questions.a: Mr Lamb uses hedging ("I should say," "to look at it") and clinical detachment, framing his tin leg as an external fact. Derry uses blunt, visceral language ("ate my face up," "ate me up") that fuses identity with injury. The contrast reveals Mr Lamb's acceptance (disability as circumstance) vs. Derry's internalization (disability as identity). A wrong answer focusing only on vocabulary difficulty misses the psychological depth board examiners reward.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "The stage directions in brackets (e.g., '[Panic]', '[Angry]', '[Pause]') are merely instructional for actors and do not contribute to literary meaning." Defend your position with two textual examples.
questions.a: The claim is false. Stage directions function as narrative commentary: "[Panic]" after Derry's "I've got to go" reveals his flight response before he speaks, shaping our reading of his subsequent defiance. "[Derry laughs a lot]" after the grim "picture fell...killed him" story signals a breakthrough — laughter as release, not amusement. Ignoring brackets treats drama as dialogue-only, losing the playwright's directorial voice that guides interpretation in board exam answers.

questions.q: Write a 4-line dialogue exchange between Derry and a new character (a curious neighbor) that uses: (a) ellipsis for hesitation, (b) a repeated interrogative for challenge, (c) an imperative redirecting attention outward, and (d) a fragment revealing internal state. Label each feature.
questions.a:
Neighbor: "So... you're the boy from the garden?" [ellipsis]
Derry: "Why do you ask? Why does everyone ask?" [repeated interrogative]
Neighbor: "Look at the sunset, not my face." [imperative redirect]
Derry: "Can't. It's all I see." [fragment]
A poor answer that writes grammatical sentences without the labeled features shows the student cannot consciously manipulate the very devices they're meant to analyze — a gap that hurts creative writing tasks in CUET.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Language Usage in the Text refers to the analysis of ______ structures, syntactic patterns, and stylistic choices the author employs in dialogue and narrative to reveal character, advance plot, and convey theme.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're overhearing two strangers talk in a park — one speaks in calm, complete ______; the other answers in sharp, broken fragments.
What is Language Usage in the Text? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Language Usage in the Text refers to the analysis of grammatical structures, syntactic patterns, and stylistic choices the author employs in dialogue and narrative to reveal character, advance plot, and convey theme.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Language Usage in the Text?
questions.a: Students believe "grammar in literature" means finding errors or labeling parts of speech (noun, verb, tense).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify and explain at least three distinct grammatical or stylistic features in the play's dialogue (e.g., ellipsis, interrogative patterns, register contrast) and analyze how each feature characterizes the speaker or develops the theme of alienation vs. connection.
